extracted.intended_audience: publishers, rights-and-permissions staff, editors, and authors (especially in scholarly and book publishing)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and contractual criteria for publishing agreements, transfers and licensing of rights, subsidiary rights management, open-access and Creative Commons considerations, permissions/clearances, and author warranties in book and journal publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic book-contract provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher undertakes to publish the book after acceptance of the manuscript and to pay the author for the rights conveyed (typically a stipulated royalty or sometimes a lump-sum fee); author grants rights and gives certain warranties and agrees to cooperate in revisions and return edited manuscripts and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book-publishing agreements are generally lengthy and detailed; common negotiation points follow (royalties, advances, acceptance standards, reversion, audit rights, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty rates and escalation points
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalty rates, including the points at which a royalty will rise, or escalate (e.g., X% on the first 10,000 copies, Y% on the next 20,000 copies, and Z% thereafter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify explicit thresholds and percentages in contract; royalty scale often negotiable and central to author compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty advances and expense allowances
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms covering royalty advances and (for certain types of books, such as textbooks) expense allowances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define payment schedule for advances and any allowable expense reimbursements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for acceptance of the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: The standards for acceptance of the manuscript, with the publisher wanting to be able to terminate the agreement if the final submitted manuscript is not 'satisfactory,' and the author wanting to limit this discretion to editorial rather than business considerations, with an opportunity to cure editorial defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract should define what 'satisfactory' means and provide author an opportunity to cure editorial defects to avoid broad business-judgment termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframe for issuing work after acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: The period following acceptance within which the publisher must issue the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify a publication window post-acceptance to prevent indefinite delays; relevant for reversion and marketing plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of rights granted to publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: What rights, beyond print rights in the publisher’s home territory (usually defined as either the US or North America) and digital rights, are granted to the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly enumerate territorial, format, and medium rights (print, ebook, audio, database, etc.) and distinguish primary from subsidiary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author indemnification obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and extent of the author’s indemnification obligations should the book turn out to violate some third party’s rights; where the publisher carries 'media perils' insurance, these obligations are most often determined with reference to the insurance coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define indemnity scope and limits; tie obligations to available insurance where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author non-compete / restriction on writing competing works
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the author’s agreement not to write a competing work, defined by subject matter and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit non-compete by clear subject-matter and audience definitions and reasonable duration to avoid overbroad restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalties for revised editions without author contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: What share of royalties the author receives for revised editions to which he or she does not contribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify percentage split or entitlement when publisher revises and reissues editions without author involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion of rights if out of print or ceases to sell
rubrics_metrics.description: How rights revert to the author if the book goes out of print or ceases to sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'out of print' and reversion mechanics (notice periods, return of rights, conditions for reversion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author audit rights
rubrics_metrics.description: On what terms the author may audit the publisher’s financial records to ensure full payment of royalties due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract should specify audit frequency, notice, scope, and who bears costs for audits revealing underpayment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify rights under Creative Commons / open-access arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book is to be published under a Creative Commons license or according to an open-access arrangement, the contract should specify exactly what rights the public is being given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the exact CC license, any CC+ addenda, and disclose to licensors of third‑party material that CC terms will apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option clauses on future works
rubrics_metrics.description: Option clauses for 'the author’s next book' or rights of first review, first refusal, or to match outstanding offers on the author’s next book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit scope (subject, character, series) and duration; these clauses are less common but material when part of a series or related titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers of rights for journal articles
rubrics_metrics.description: When an article is accepted for publication in a scholarly journal, the publisher usually asks the author to sign a formal transfer of rights in the contribution; where multiple authors exist, lead author may sign with a representation of authority to bind coauthors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain to authors that without broad transfers publishers cannot license anthologies, databases, classroom copying, or other subsidiary uses; fair provisions return limited reprint rights to authors (e.g., reprinting in scholarly works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailored (less-than-full) licenses for journal content
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journal publishers, when an author refuses to transfer copyright in toto, ask instead for a license more closely tailored to their specific needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure such licenses cover all subsidiary rights the publisher may want to exercise or sublicense and are exclusive where needed (especially for electronic/database rights); keep careful records of rights granted per article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor copyright in collective works
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the editor is an employee or agent of the company or society that owns the journal, the editor has a separate copyright in each issue as a collective work; ownership should be clearly agreed on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify ownership and rights of the editor versus publisher in contracts to avoid later disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreements for edited compilations and chapter contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Edited books (chapters by various authors) require contracts reflecting allocation of responsibilities between editor and contributors; editors as authors of the collective work should sign appropriate agreements; simpler forms closer to journal author forms may be used for contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify standard author agreements for contributor royalty shares, responsibilities, and work-made-for-hire where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts for symposium proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings published as journal issues or stand-alone books, clarify who owns copyright in the editor’s work and secure from every contributor a contract similar to article author forms or chapter contributor forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send and file signed contributor forms with the publisher’s contract for the volume; treat proceedings editor like a book editor for contracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theses and dissertations repository and embargo rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Many institutions require theses/dissertations submitted to an electronic repository; authors usually retain copyright and may be able to limit access or embargo the full text for a specified period while abstracts remain public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must understand institutional requirements and implications for reuse in subsequent publications; obtain permissions for third-party copyrighted material beyond fair use and be prepared to submit documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green versus gold open-access models
rubrics_metrics.description: Green open access: author retains or secures right to deposit a manuscript in an open-access repository (often after embargo); Gold open access: author grants publisher right to make the published version immediately available open-access, typically supported by institutional subsidy or page charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Green usually costs publisher little; gold often requires subsidy or author charges; both accompanied by special licenses and have different economic impacts on publisher revenue streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Commons license types and publisher cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Six basic CC licenses (CC BY; CC BY-SA; CC BY-ND; CC BY-NC; CC BY-NC-SA; CC BY-NC-ND) range from least to most restrictive, varying by attribution, share-alike, derivative, and noncommercial clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should approach CC with caution (consider adding noncommercial or no-derivatives clauses), ensure authors have clearances for third-party material, and disclose CC terms to any licensor of included material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-publishing service agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-publishing platforms require standard contracts; under such contracts, the author generally retains copyright and sets the price within limits; contracts tend to be nonexclusive but may offer exclusive options with special terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors usually cannot self-publish works under contract with a traditional publisher unless they retained rights; self-publishing does not necessarily preclude future traditional publication and agreements can generally be terminated by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of subsidiary rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsidiary rights commonly include original-language territorial rights, translation rights, serial rights (first/second), paperback rights, book-club rights, reprint rights, Braille/accessibility editions, dramatic rights, audio rights, electronic rights, enhanced electronic rights, scholarly use rights, educational use rights, microform, abstracting, and document-delivery reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish which are primary vs subsidiary for the contract at issue; consider territory, media, and whether electronic rights are primary for publisher-issued e-books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and derivative-work copyright considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation rights license a publisher in another territory to translate and exercise standard publisher’s rights; copyright in the translation as a derivative work belongs initially to the translator or to the publisher of the translation, though license can impose restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract terms should address ownership of translation copyright, restrictions on exercise, and sublicensing limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic rights and enhanced electronic rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic rights cover sale in e-book format, inclusion in databases, and other electronic uses; enhanced electronic rights involve adding hyperlinks, video, and other substantial features creating derivative works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether electronic rights are primary or subsidiary; assign new ISBNs for electronic versions; specifically obtain rights to enhance the electronic text if general derivative rights are not granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic-rights licensing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether licensing to aggregators, research services, and library-borrowing platforms will augment or 'cannibalize' print sales; ensure delivery mechanisms have safeguards against excessive downloading/copying (digital rights management); generally grant electronic licenses for limited multi-year terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess economic and strategic trade-offs; include DRM and duration terms; revisit frequently due to rapid change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' electronic use of their own works
rubrics_metrics.description: Author rights to post or otherwise use their own works electronically are contentious: password-protected campus sites may be acceptable, while open posting on personal or institutional websites can undercut licensing revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should weigh goodwill from author flexibility against revenue risks; trend is toward greater open access but publishers may negotiate manuscript vs final-version posting and embargo periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: University license addenda pitfalls and publisher responses
rubrics_metrics.description: University policies/presumptive nonexclusive licenses to post faculty articles for noncommercial uses can create problematic addenda that fail to clarify derivative rights, distinguishing manuscript vs published version, or preventing licensing to 'noncommercial' competing journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should develop their own addenda granting limited rights (internal use, manuscript posting, final published version after a delay) to address university requests while protecting publisher interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-access policies (e.g., NIH Public Access Policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some government agencies require submission of final manuscripts of peer-reviewed articles derived from funded research to public repositories (e.g., NIH requires posting on PubMed Central upon final acceptance, and articles must be posted no later than twelve months after official publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such policies are mandatory (not opt-out) and contracts must stipulate the timing for public posting; publishers may substitute their published versions but will typically push for maximum allowable embargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic handling of subsidiary-rights income
rubrics_metrics.description: When the publisher sells or licenses rights to others, proceeds are paid in lump sum or royalty and normally split between publisher and author according to contract (typical book agreement author receives at least 50 percent of such income).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid suspect 'sweetheart' arrangements licensing at artificially low royalties to affiliates; treat licenses between related companies like those to unrelated companies unless author agrees otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling permissions requests and rights database management
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should have rights-and-permissions staff to handle requests and a complete accurate rights database recording what rights the publisher has and any conditions restricting licenseability (e.g., author approval required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights database is prerequisite to efficient and legally safe permissions programs, especially where third-party materials are embedded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author copyright warranties
rubrics_metrics.description: Author warrants that the work is original, that the author owns it, that no part has been previously published, that no other agreement to publish it or part is outstanding, and that any copyrighted material of other authors used in the work is used with permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indemnification often backs these warranties; unless publisher agrees otherwise, the burden falls on the author to secure permissions except where fair use applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warranties about defamation, invasion of privacy, accuracy, and injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Author should warrant the work does not libel anyone or infringe privacy; may be asked to warrant that no instructions will cause injury and sometimes that factual statements are accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher should query author on material posing defamation/privacy risks; courts are hesitant to impose liability for inaccurate advice, but publishers remain cautious from reputational and legal standpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of counsel in rights and content review
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel versed in relevant law can review passages of concern (permission needs, defamation risk) and should have direct communication with the author provided it is clear counsel represents the publisher, not the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow counsel’s suggestions for manuscript changes absent compelling reasons to the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles for obtaining permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must obtain permission to use copyrighted material created by others unless the use is 'fair use'; permission should be in writing; no permission is needed for US government works or works for which copyright has expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that modern editions/translations/introductions may be copyrighted even when original text is public domain; as good practice always credit sources and be prepared to submit permissions documentation with the paper.
